1.pericope_label: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry. And he prayed unto the Lord, and said, I pray thee, O Lord, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil
debates: What Jonah was actually angry about
Whether what he says here is a prayer at all
outliers: Calvin dismisses an older reading that made the grief a holy zeal for Israel
Gill finds nothing of true prayer in the speech at all
Keil and Delitzsch contrasts the reason Elijah gave for the same request
themes: A man angry at the thing angels rejoice over
Anger described as a burning
A prayer with none of the parts of prayer
The best intention condemned from God’s own mouth

3.pericope_label: Therefore now, O Lord, take, I beseech thee, my life from me; for it is better for me to die than to live. Then said the Lord, Doest thou well to be angry? So Jonah went out of the city, and sat on the east side of the city, and there made him a booth, and sat under it in the shadow, till he might see what would become of the city
debates: How the question put to Jonah should be rendered
Whether Jonah left the city before or after the forty days
Whether his wish to die can be excused
outliers: Ellicott notes that none of these men who loathed life ever contemplated suicide
Clarke says an angry preacher should not be an overseer in God’s house
Calvin asks how Jonah could have known the outcome before the fortieth day
themes: A man asking God for the death he will not take himself
A question left with a man to consider
A booth of boughs on the east side of a city
Strife let out like water through a breach

6.pericope_label: And the Lord God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head, to deliver him from his grief. So Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd. But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered
debates: What plant the Hebrew word names
Whether the plant grew miraculously or had been growing already
Whether so small a thing as a worm falls under providence
outliers: Calvin faults both sides of an ancient quarrel over how to translate the word
Ellicott quotes a naturalist who prefers the gourd on practical grounds
Gill objects to a father who professed ignorance of who made worms
themes: A shade that grows overnight
Leaves as broad as the rim of a hat
Fruit hanging from leafless tendrils after a storm
A worm at the root by daybreak

8.pericope_label: And it came to pass, when the sun did arise, that God prepared a vehement east wind; and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted, and wished in himself to die, and said, It is better for me to die than to live. And God said to Jonah, Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd? And he said, I do well to be angry, even unto death
debates: Whether the east wind was a quiet or a boisterous one
Why the question names the plant and not the wind or the sun
What Jonah’s case shows about the gifts of prophecy
outliers: Ellicott notes that Jonah takes the worthier excuse the moment it is offered him
Clarke traces the eye disease of Egypt to the sand these winds carry
Calvin says God anticipated a man who was seeking his own destruction
themes: A wind whose name means silent
Suffering of the body deepening a grief of the mind
A question that leaves out the worst of the trouble
A gift that leaves the heart unchanged

10.pericope_label: Then said the Lord, Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?
debates: Whether the comparison of plant and city really holds
Whether those who cannot tell right hand from left are children or the ignorant
What the mention of the cattle is doing at the end
outliers: Calvin raises the objection to the comparison himself before answering it
Calvin rejects a reading that would count the ignorant rather than infants, citing the size of Paris
Ellicott calls the clause about the cattle the most striking thing in the book
themes: A shade valued more than a city
A plant that was son of a night and perished a son of a night
Children who cannot tell one hand from the other
Cattle counted among the reasons for mercy
